compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
Two staff members handling the same complaint may both explain the policy clearly and follow through. Training, experience and a shared procedure can help explain that similarity. A preference code cannot establish who is more dependable.

compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
Two staff members handling the same complaint may both explain the policy clearly and follow through. Training, experience and a shared procedure can help explain that similarity. A preference code cannot establish who is more dependable.

E concerns where people tend to direct attention and energy. S concerns the concrete details and experiences that stand out. J concerns structure in the outside world. None establishes how quickly someone can close a case.

Look at the reasons for a decision to understand the T/F distinction. One reason might be that a policy should apply consistently across similar cases. Another might be that a decision should take account of the disruption to this customer. A member of staff could use both reasons in the same decision.

### ### ESFJ and ESTJ: two reasons for the same complaint decision

In a fictional store, a customer returns with a rice cooker whose inner coating has started to peel. They bought it eleven days ago and ask to return it and be reimbursed for travel. Both staff members see the same receipt and return policy. They can both recommend an exception, but only a supervisor can approve one. The invented policy explains the scenario only.

One reason to recommend an exception is the verified cost and disruption to the customer. Another is a gap in the policy that would affect comparable complaints. The first highlights personal impact, and the second highlights consistent criteria. Either staff member can document both.

Both might recommend the same outcome, including processing the return and asking a supervisor to review the travel request. If they consider only the impact on this customer, treatment may vary across similar cases. If they consider only the existing rule, a gap in the policy may go unnoticed.

Either person could start by reviewing the receipt or listening to the customer. A procedure may require one step before the other. The examples illustrate reasons someone could weigh and do not identify a type from the order of actions.

### ### ESFJ and ESTJ: why their dominant and inferior functions differ

For both extraverted types, J indicates that the outward-facing dominant function is a judging process. ESFJ has F, so its dominant function is extraverted Feeling (Fe) and its inferior function is introverted Thinking (Ti). ESTJ has T, so its dominant function is extraverted Thinking (Te) and its inferior function is introverted Feeling (Fi). Both have auxiliary introverted Sensing (Si).

Both also have Intuition in the third position in the model. Changing F to T changes the judging processes, while the two perceiving processes keep their positions. The stack describes this relationship between preferences and cannot rank the quality of anyone’s judgment.

This article uses extraverted Intuition (Ne) in the third position for both types. The Foundation also lists introverted Intuition (Ni) as an option there. compare_blocks.body:
The following fictional examples illustrate how people may explain a decision. They do not state what any store or building must do in a real case.

Two colleagues may agree on the evidence and still emphasise different reasons. Ask what one person wants the decision to do for those affected and what the other wants it to do across similar cases. Often the request can be evaluated on both grounds.

### ### ESFJ and ESTJ: reviewing the rice cooker return

In the fictional rice cooker case, both employees can process the same return under the store’s terms and recommend an exception for travel expenses. The supervisor decides on the exception.

One note might focus on the documented trips and disruption to the household. Another might focus on how the same travel request would be assessed next time. Both employees can write both points in the same note.

Even if they both recommend reimbursement, one might cite the verified effect on the customer and the other a consistent rule for previously uncovered cases. The same recommendation can reflect either or both reasons.

Record the decision separately from its rationale, including what facts are confirmed and who is responsible for reviewing any exception.

For a review, group cases by whether they fall within the policy, were referred for review or were closed without a referral. Check whether comparable cases were treated consistently and whether the reasons account for the people affected. This reviews the process rather than anyone’s personality.

### ### ESFJ and ESTJ: explaining the same repair estimate

In a fictional repair shop, a customer brings in a washing machine that makes a rattling sound. Both employees have the same inspection fee, estimated parts prices, turnaround and loan appliance terms. Both have the same discretion to waive the inspection fee.

One consideration is what being without the machine would mean for the household, including whether a loan appliance would help. Another is how the fee and price range follow the same criteria used for other repairs. Either employee could include both considerations.

Explain which figures and dates are estimates and which commitments the shop can make. Either type can clarify whether parts availability will change the cost or the timing.

Both employees could decide to waive the fee or explain why it applies. The role, information and reasons matter more than whether the person used a sympathetic tone.

### ### ESFJ and ESTJ: discussing late-evening music practice

In a fictional apartment building, a child practices music late in the evening. Two neighbours have the same building guidance on quiet hours and can contact the household or building management. Neither has enforcement authority.

One consideration is how a change in practice time would affect the neighbouring households and the child. Another is how the quiet-hours guidance applies to similar situations. Both neighbours can consider those questions together.

They might agree to contact the same person and still have different reasons for doing so. The choice of whom to contact first tells you little about T/F.

If they raise the issue, it helps to describe when the noise occurred, how long it lasted and what it disrupted. That gives the recipient something specific to respond to.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
Thinking and Feeling describe considerations in a judgment. Someone who values consistency can care about the effects on a customer, and someone who weighs those effects can apply a rule consistently. Tone alone tells you little about the reasons.

Store managers and customer service supervisors may be trained to speak about different parts of the same problem. The job title gives no basis for assigning a type.

Accurately explaining a policy and understanding what a customer needs are relevant skills. Either person can learn and use both.

A case can take longer because the needed records are missing, an approval is pending or the store is busy. Speed and the number of questions asked do not establish a T/F preference.

sections.body_md:
Two staff members handling the same complaint may both explain the policy clearly and follow through. Training, experience and a shared procedure can help explain that similarity. A preference code cannot establish who is more dependable.

E concerns where people tend to direct attention and energy. S concerns the concrete details and experiences that stand out. J concerns structure in the outside world. None establishes how quickly someone can close a case.

Look at the reasons for a decision to understand the T/F distinction. One reason might be that a policy should apply consistently across similar cases. In a fictional store, a customer returns with a rice cooker whose inner coating has started to peel. They bought it eleven days ago and ask to return it and be reimbursed for travel. Both staff members see the same receipt and return policy. They can both recommend an exception, but only a supervisor can approve one. The invented policy explains the scenario only.

ESFJ has F, so its dominant function is extraverted Feeling (Fe) and its inferior function is introverted Thinking (Ti).
